languages.note: Mandarin lacks 'th' sounds and has no final voiced stops; 'l' and 'n' and the English 'r' are frequently confused, and short/long vowel contrasts are hard.
Spanish has five pure vowels, so English lax vowels (ɪ, æ, ʌ, ʊ) tend to collapse into nearby tense vowels; 'b/v' and 's/z' are often merged.
Hindi merges 'v' and 'w' into one sound, replaces 'th' with dental stops, and uses retroflex 't/d' that color English alveolar stops.
Arabic lacks 'p' (often realized as 'b') and 'v', has only three vowel qualities so short English vowels are hard, and tends to insert vowels into consonant clusters.
Korean has no 'f/v/z/th', uses one liquid for 'l' and 'r', and tends to add a vowel after final consonants, breaking clusters.
Japanese has a single tap for 'l' and 'r', lacks 'th' and 'v', and its open-syllable structure leads to extra vowels inserted into consonant clusters.
French has no 'th' or 'h', uses a uvular 'r', and stresses syllables evenly, which flattens English word stress and rhythm.
German devoices final consonants (so 'd' sounds like 't'), lacks 'th', confuses 'w' and 'v', and uses a different 'r'.
Portuguese lacks 'th', nasalizes vowels heavily, uses an 'h'-like or guttural 'r', and often turns dark final 'l' into a 'w'-like sound.
Russian has no 'th' or 'w' (often replaced by 'v'), devoices final consonants, uses a trilled 'r', and reduces unstressed vowels differently from English schwa.
